To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the public wants to be involved in the governance of biobanking projects, wants more control over the use of their samples and data, and is concerned with potential misuse by third parties.

1) the majority of the public is interested, and willing to provide consent, for the use of their data in research; 2) the majority of respondents prefer a one-time general informed consent to the future use and sharing of their biological samples and data among researchers; and 3) respondents’ concerns about biotechnology and biobanking generally centre on issues related to the control and ownership and misuse of their biological samples by third parties.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how the public perceives the objectives, structure and governance of biobanks and the control and ownership issues that arise when biological samples and data are shared.
how the public views the sharing of data and samples, and the ethical implications of these views.
the public’s perceptions about how their biological samples and data are used in biobanking.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the public is generally in favour of biobanking, but that there are significant concerns that need to be addressed.
there are many issues to consider in the governance of biobanks, but the Canadian public appears to be willing to share their samples and data if given appropriate information and a sense of control.
the Canadian public is willing to participate in biobanking, but only if they are provided with sufficient information and have a say in how the project is run.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the public is generally supportive of biobanking, provided that they are adequately informed about the project, its objectives, the governance structure and accountability.
the public wants to know that they have some control over how their data is used, and that their data will not be used for commercial purposes, and that their privacy is protected.
there is no clear public preference for a specific model of consent for the sharing of samples and data among researchers.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Canadian public wants to be involved and wants to know how their information is being used.
the public has a nuanced and informed view on the issues surrounding biobanking and that the current consent process should be improved to better address their concerns.
the public wants to be well-informed about biobanking projects.
